stops.name: Pamplona, the king-trouvère laid in Santa María
stops.campa: The king-trouvère dies at Pamplona in July, and Joffrey crosses the mountains a last time to see him laid in Santa María. The songs do not die with him; they escaped long ago into the mouths of two kingdoms. Standing at the tomb, the seneschal reckons his own accounts: two crusades, three entries into Jerusalem, one treaty signed at Jaffa, one rose alive at Provins, one well, one tower, one tree. The melody, he decides, carried further than the sword, and he goes home to prove it to children.

stops.name: The tree: dragons, the Rock beneath the Dome, and the portal
stops.campa: On Saint John's Eve, by the fires, the old lord tells the children of the tree his adventures in the Holy Land: the Rock beneath the Dome, the crib at Greccio, the seraph of the five wounds, and the dragons of the forest, whom he has promoted from rumour to neighbours. The children laugh at the old man, and cherish his protection, and his residence inside the fiction. For this place is a portal of Celtic magic, a home for the fairies, and it keeps an adolescent spirit that will one day save France.

stops.name: Château de Bourlémont, the death of the seneschal
stops.campa: In the year 1268 Joffrey de Bourlémont dies in his rebuilt castle, an old crusader of fifty-seven, Sibylle's husband, the king's seneschal, the children's dragon-keeper. The lordship passes on; the charter sleeps at Mureau; the well keeps its water and the tower its view. Of his long errand the valley keeps what valleys keep: three stones, one story, and a tree that has learned the names of things it intends to remember for two hundred years, until a scribe and a spinner of light are born to receive them.

stops.name: Neufchâteau: Lois de Conte, two hundred years after
stops.campa: Lois de Conte is born at Neufchâteau on the sixth of January, two hundred years after Joffrey, on his very feast of the Kings. Sent to Domremy after a raid of Burgundian bandits, he is taught his letters by the priest Guillaume Fronte and becomes the scribe of the Children of the Tree: the same dance, the same beech, the same well and tower. Among the five children of Jacques and Isabelle he grows closest to Joan, who shares his birthday. The legacy has found its clerk, and the clerk has found his subject.

stops.name: The tree, Joan's garlands at the well
stops.campa: Joan sings and dances with the children around the old beech, weaves garlands of flowers and herbs and leaves them for the fairies on the boughs and at Joffrey's spring. Her godmother has told her the romance of the tree: that in old times a lord of Bourlémont met a lady called Fée beneath it and they talked together. She drinks from the well the old crusader built for children he did not yet know. The tree that heard the dragons and the Rock beneath the Dome begins, very quietly, to answer.

stops.name: The tower, Saint Barbara and the black window
stops.campa: The tower stands locked now, but Joan claims access by night. Within it she communes with Saint Barbara, the maiden of the tower, who teaches her the science of artillery and how to open portals. She tells Lois of her hair standing on end, of a black window opening in the wall framed by brilliant lightning, of being one and the same with Barbara and with all the maidens of the tower who are spinning thread of light. Joffrey's stone chair of grief has become an engine of annunciation, exactly as the field intended.

stops.name: The tree, the testimony of the fairy
stops.campa: At the Rehabilitation inquiry, before the notaries at Domremy, Joan's godmother, Jeanne, widow of Thiesselin de Vittel, testifies to the romance she once told the child: that in ancient times the lord Pierre de Bourlément and a lady named Fée met beneath this tree and conversed together. The family's name and the fairy enter the parchment record wed under the boughs. The well gives water; the children still dance; and the fire Joffrey carried home from Greccio and Jerusalem has done exactly what he told them it would.
